claim: A total of 11,284 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were detected, of which 4549 (40.3%) were identified as terrestrial invertebrates.
source: We detected a total of 11,284 operational taxonomic units (OTUs), of which 4549 (40.3%) were identified as terrestrial invertebrates.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement results from DNA metabarcoding analysis

claim: The terrestrial invertebrate OTUs mostly belonged to the phylum Arthropoda (2,626 OTUs, among which insects were most common), followed by Rotifera (772 OTUs), Nematoda (656 OTUs), Mollusca (219 OTUs), Annelida (204 OTUs), Platyhelminthes (44 OTUs), Tardigrada (22 OTUs), Gastrotricha (four OTUs), and Onychophora (two OTUs).
source: The terrestrial invertebrate OTUs mostly belonged to the phylum Arthropoda (2,626 OTUs, among which insects were most common), followed by Rotifera (772 OTUs), Nematoda (656 OTUs), Mollusca (219 OTUs), Annelida (204 OTUs), Platyhelminthes (44 OTUs), Tardigrada (22 OTUs), Gastrotricha (four OTUs), and Onychophora (two OTUs) (Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
evidence: Direct statement of taxonomic composition from DNA metabarcoding data

claim: Natural forest samples formed a distinct cluster with no overlap with any other land-use categories in non-metric MDS ordinations.
source: Natural forest samples formed a distinct cluster with no overlap with any other land-use categories.
evidence: Observation from MDS ordination analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: PERMANOVA tests detected a significant difference in overall invertebrate community composition among different land-use categories (F4,61 = 1.804, p≤0.001).
source: PERMANOVA tests for composition differences among different land-use categories detected a significant difference based on the overall invertebrate community (F4,61 = 1.804, p≤0.001), and based on each of the main phyla detected (Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Nematoda and Rotifera; F4,44-61 = 1.447–2.288, p≤0.001; Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: Statistical test results from PERMANOVA analysis

claim: Multivariate heterogeneity of sample dispersions, mean pairwise beta diversity, and mean pairwise phylogenetic beta diversity were highest in natural forest sites and lowest in grassland and/or cropland sites.
source: For overall invertebrate communities, each of these measures differed significantly among land uses (F4, 61-442 = 3.59–14.99, p≤0.011), being highest in natural forest sites and lowest in grassland and/or cropland sites (Figure 1—source data 1B; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Statistical test results and figure references showing beta diversity patterns

claim: Low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland samples each had relatively consistent assemblages of abundant OTUs, both within and between each land-use category.
source: A heatmap based on the 1000 most relatively abundant terrestrial invertebrate OTUs detected suggested that low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland samples each had relatively consistent assemblages of abundant OTUs, both within and between each land-use category, whereas planted forest samples, and especially natural forest samples, each had more distinctive assemblages of abundant OTUs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from heatmap analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Most natural forest samples had a subset of abundant OTUs that were not detected in any other sample.
source: In particular, most of the natural forest samples had a subset of abundant OTUs that were not detected in any other sample.
evidence: Observation from heatmap analysis

claim: Rarity and phylogenetic rarity metrics showed the largest and most consistent land-use-related biodiversity declines.
source: Rarity and phylogenetic rarity metrics showed the largest and most consistent land-use-related biodiversity declines, with the highest mean values in natural forest sites followed by planted forest sites and low-producing grassland sites, and high-producing grassland sites, and lowest values in perennial cropland sites.
evidence: Summary of biodiversity metric patterns across land uses shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Significant differences between mean biodiversity of overall invertebrate communities in different land-use categories were detected according to richness, rarity, phylogenetic diversity, phylogenetic rarity, and phylogenetic diversity and rarity SES metrics.
source: Significant differences between mean biodiversity of overall invertebrate communities in different land-use categories were detected according to richness, rarity, phylogenetic diversity, phylogenetic rarity, and phylogenetic diversity and rarity SES metrics (F4,64 = 3.56 to 17.986, p = 0.012 to <0.001), but not effective species numbers, mean pairwise distance, or mean pairwise distance SES metrics (Figure 3—source data 1A; Figure 4—source data 1A).
evidence: ANOVA test results for biodiversity metrics

claim: The mean rarity of overall invertebrate communities was significantly lower in all four other land uses compared with natural forest.
source: The mean rarity of overall invertebrate communities was significantly lower in all four other land uses compared with natural forest (t23-27 = −31.6 to −62.4, P.adj = 0.03 to <0.001).
evidence: Post-hoc Tukey HSD test results

claim: The mean phylogenetic rarity of overall invertebrate communities was significantly lower in all four other land-use categories compared with natural forest.
source: Similarly, the mean phylogenetic rarity of overall invertebrate communities was significantly lower in all four other land-use categories compared with natural forest (t23-27 = −3.34 to −6.90, P.adj = 0.043 to <0.001), and in perennial cropland compared with planted forest (t24 = −3.55, P.adj = 0.046).
evidence: Post-hoc Tukey HSD test results

claim: Derived land-use rank and taxonomic group were the most consistently significant predictors of the diversity metrics.
source: A mixed-model ANOVA test for effects of derived land-use rank, land-use category, and taxonomic group effects showed that derived land-use rank and taxonomic group (and interactions) were the most consistently significant predictors of the diversity metrics (F1-16 = 7.74 to 32.14, p = 0.007 to <0.001; Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: Mixed-model ANOVA test results

claim: Most environmental variables showed clear land use-related trends of increasing or decreasing values in the order of natural forest, planted forest, low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland.
source: Most environmental variables showed clear land use-related trends of increasing or decreasing values in the order of natural forest, planted forest, low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: Observation from environmental variable analysis

claim: Latitude had no effect on overall soil invertebrate biodiversity according to any metric.
source: An ANOVA test of spatial attributes (latitude and altitude) plus land-use category showed latitude had no effect on overall soil invertebrate biodiversity according to any metric, whereas altitude had significant effects on biodiversity of all metrics except for mean pairwise distance (F1 = 9.41 to 22.33, p = 0.003 to <0.001).
evidence: ANOVA test results for spatial attributes

claim: Altitude had significant effects on biodiversity of all metrics except for mean pairwise distance.
source: An ANOVA test of spatial attributes (latitude and altitude) plus land-use category showed latitude had no effect on overall soil invertebrate biodiversity according to any metric, whereas altitude had significant effects on biodiversity of all metrics except for mean pairwise distance (F1 = 9.41 to 22.33, p = 0.003 to <0.001).
evidence: ANOVA test results for spatial attributes

claim: ANOVA tests detected significant differences among land-use categories for ten of the 17 taxonomic groups based on rarity.
source: ANOVA tests detected significant differences among land-use categories for ten of the 17 taxonomic groups based on rarity (all insect groups, non-mites, Annelida, Nematoda, and Platyhelminthes; F4 = 2.60 to 13.26, p = 0.048 to <0.001); nine groups based both on phylogenetic rarity (all insect groups except Hemiptera, mites and non-mites, Annelida, and Platyhelminthes; F4 = 2.74 to 11.07, p = 0.036 to <0.001) and phylogenetic diversity (all insect groups, Annelida, Mollusca, and Nematoda; F4 = 3.14 to 6.41, p = 0.047 to <0.001); eight groups based on richness (all insect groups, Nematoda, and Platyhelminthes; F4 = 2.55 to 6.32, p = 0.048 to <0.001); five groups based on effective species numbers (Diptera, Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, mites, and Annelida; F4 = 2.73 to 4.36, p = 0.037 to 0.004); and three groups based on mean pairwise distance differences (Hymenoptera, mites, and Rotifera; F4 = 3.53 to 6.24, p = 0.012 to <0.001; Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: ANOVA test results for taxonomic groups

claim: Non-parametric bootstrapping showed that phylogenetic rarity followed by (non-phylogenetic) rarity explained the largest proportions of land-use category variance across the 17 taxonomic groups.
source: Non-parametric bootstrapping of ANOVA sum of squares values for the (non-SES) biodiversity metrics and taxonomic groups for which significant land-use differences were detected showed that phylogenetic rarity followed by (non-phylogenetic) rarity explained the largest proportions of land-use category variance across the 17 taxonomic groups, while mean pairwise distance and richness explained the least variance (Figure 5).
evidence: Bootstrapping analysis results shown in Figure 5

claim: A Kruskal-Wallis test detected significant differences among the biodiversity metrics (Chi square = 4782.6, df = 5, p<0.001).
source: A Kruskal-Wallis test detected significant differences among the biodiversity metrics (Chi square = 4782.6, df = 5, p<0.001), with post-hoc tests indicating that the distributions of all metrics differed significantly from each other (p<0.05).
evidence: Kruskal-Wallis test results

claim: ANOVA tests detected significant differences among land-use categories for 11 of the 17 taxonomic groups based on phylogenetic rarity SES.
source: ANOVA tests detected significant differences among land-use categories for 11 of the 17 taxonomic groups based on phylogenetic rarity SES (Collembola, Coleoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, other insects, mites and non-mites, Annelida, Mollusca, Nematoda, and Rotifera; F4 = 3.10 to 8.91, p = 0.022 to <0.001), six groups based on phylogenetic diversity SES (Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, mites, Malacostraca, Nematoda, and Rotifera; F4 = 2.76 to 7.39, p = 0.035 to <0.001); and four groups based on mean pairwise distance SES (Lepidoptera, mites, Malacostraca, and Rotifera; F4 = 4.40 to 11.28, p = 0.016 to <0.001; Figure 4—source data 1B).
evidence: ANOVA test results for phylogenetic SES metrics

claim: All of the 11 taxonomic groups with significant phylogenetic rarity SES differences showed a consistent pattern of declining rarity from natural forest to planted forest to agricultural land-use categories.
source: All of the 11 taxonomic groups with significant phylogenetic rarity SES differences showed a consistent pattern of declining rarity from natural forest to planted forest to agricultural land-use categories.
evidence: Summary of phylogenetic rarity SES patterns across taxonomic groups

claim: Rarity metrics were much more sensitive to land use and more consistent among taxa than richness or effective species numbers.
source: However, rarity metrics were much more sensitive to land use and more consistent among taxa than richness or effective species numbers in our study, suggesting that the latter metrics may underestimate land-use impacts on biodiversity.
evidence: Synthesis of results comparing different biodiversity metrics

claim: Rarity is a function of the number of species with limited distributions or narrow habitat specificity.
source: Rarity is a function of the number of species with limited distributions or narrow habitat specificity.
evidence: Definition of rarity metric based on established methodology

claim: Rare species can have important roles in ecosystem processes.
source: These rare species can have important roles in ecosystem processes (Dee et al., 2019; Leitão et al., 2016; Lyons et al., 2005), and are inherently more vulnerable to extinction.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Rare species are inherently more vulnerable to extinction.
source: These rare species can have important roles in ecosystem processes (Dee et al., 2019; Leitão et al., 2016; Lyons et al., 2005), and are inherently more vulnerable to extinction.
evidence: Statement based on ecological knowledge

claim: Rare plant and fungal species appear to be particularly sensitive to changes in environment.
source: For example, rare plant and fungal species appear to be particularly sensitive to changes in environment (Avis et al., 2008; Dickie et al., 2009; Dickie and Reich, 2005; McIntyre and Lavorel, 1994), and pollinating insect losses are concentrated among rare species (Powney et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Pollinating insect losses are concentrated among rare species.
source: For example, rare plant and fungal species appear to be particularly sensitive to changes in environment (Avis et al., 2008; Dickie et al., 2009; Dickie and Reich, 2005; McIntyre and Lavorel, 1994), and pollinating insect losses are concentrated among rare species (Powney et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research

claim: Most of the terrestrial invertebrate species currently considered to be at risk or threat of extinction in New Zealand are naturally uncommon.
source: Furthermore, most of the terrestrial invertebrate species currently considered to be at risk or threat of extinction in New Zealand are naturally uncommon (Stringer and Hitchmough, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research

claim: Phylogenetic diversity – and especially phylogenetic rarity – explained larger proportions of land-use variance across taxa than their non-phylogenetic counterparts.
source: Phylogenetic diversity – and especially phylogenetic rarity – explained larger proportions of land-use variance across taxa than their non-phylogenetic counterparts, and phylogenetic rarity was overall the most sensitive metric to land-use differences.
evidence: Summary of comparative analysis of biodiversity metrics

claim: Phylogenetic rarity was overall the most sensitive metric to land-use differences.
source: Phylogenetic diversity – and especially phylogenetic rarity – explained larger proportions of land-use variance across taxa than their non-phylogenetic counterparts, and phylogenetic rarity was overall the most sensitive metric to land-use differences.
evidence: Summary of comparative analysis of biodiversity metrics

claim: Phylogenetic metrics incorporate evolutionary and functional aspects of biodiversity.
source: Phylogenetic metrics incorporate evolutionary and functional aspects of biodiversity (Faith, 1992; Faith, 2015; Mazel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: New Zealand has a long history of geographic isolation and glaciation, reflected by the presence of many deeply divergent invertebrate lineages.
source: New Zealand has a long history of geographic isolation and glaciation, reflected by the presence of many deeply divergent invertebrate lineages (Buckley et al., 2015; Trewick et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: The high levels of invertebrate phylogenetic rarity in natural forest sites likely reflects assemblages of long-present soil invertebrates that are highly adapted to these habitats, but ill-suited to the modified land-use types included in the study.
source: The high levels of invertebrate phylogenetic rarity in natural forest sites likely reflects assemblages of long-present soil invertebrates that are highly adapted to these habitats, but ill-suited to the modified land-use types included in the study.
evidence: Interpretation of phylogenetic rarity patterns based on ecological reasoning

claim: The low beta diversity, heterogeneity, and rarity values detected in agricultural sites, and the overlap of samples from these sites in MDS ordinations, together strongly imply that these habitats tend to have relatively similar assemblages of species across locations.
source: The low beta diversity, heterogeneity, and rarity values detected in agricultural sites, and the overlap of samples from these sites in MDS ordinations, together strongly imply that these habitats tend to have relatively similar assemblages of species across locations.
evidence: Interpretation of multiple biodiversity metrics and ordination results

claim: Agricultural practices have effects at a wide range of scales, from local-scale use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides to landscape-scale habitat simplification.
source: Agricultural practices have effects at a wide range of scales, from local-scale use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides to landscape-scale habitat simplification (Tscharntke et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research

claim: Agricultural practices lead to homogenisation of communities and functions among sites, in which specialists in diverse natural communities are replaced by a smaller number of generalists that thrive in anthropogenic habitats.
source: Together these factors lead to homogenisation of communities and functions among sites, in which specialists in diverse natural communities are replaced by a smaller number of generalists that thrive in anthropogenic habitats (Börschig et al., 2013; Clavel et al., 2011; Gámez-Virués et al., 2015; McKinney and Lockwood, 1999; Smart et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: The high diversity and rarity observed in natural forest sites indicates that these habitats tend to have richer and more unique assemblages of species.
source: In contrast to the agricultural sites, the high diversity and rarity observed in natural forest sites indicates that these habitats tend to have richer and more unique assemblages of species.
evidence: Interpretation of biodiversity metric results

claim: Forested sites tend to have greater physical habitat complexity and heterogeneity, providing more varied resources and niches for diverse communities including various specialists.
source: Forested sites tend to have greater physical habitat complexity and heterogeneity, providing more varied resources and niches for diverse communities including various specialists (Jonsson et al., 2009; Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Natural forest habitats tend to be more disconnected, and located in more rugged and less accessible areas than agricultural sites, with more physical barriers to limit the dispersal of invertebrate fauna.
source: Furthermore, natural forest habitats tend to be more disconnected, and located in more rugged and less accessible areas than agricultural sites, with more physical barriers to limit the dispersal of invertebrate fauna.
evidence: Statement based on ecological knowledge and geographic characteristics

claim: The distinct assemblages detected in natural forest sites are likely to reflect natural historical biogeographic distribution and evolutionary processes.
source: Consequently, the distinct assemblages detected in natural forest sites are likely to reflect natural historical biogeographic distribution and evolutionary processes (Buckley et al., 2015; Trewick et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior research

claim: Most metrics of rarity and diversity (not mean pairwise distance, phylogenetic diversity SES, or mean pairwise distance SES) showed a consistent trend of lower biodiversity in agricultural land-use categories than in forested land-use categories.
source: Despite their varying sensitivity, most metrics of rarity and diversity (not mean pairwise distance, phylogenetic diversity SES, or mean pairwise distance SES) showed a consistent trend of lower biodiversity in agricultural land-use categories than in forested land-use categories.
evidence: Summary of biodiversity metric patterns across land uses

claim: While not all taxa showed significant evidence of declining biodiversity in relation to agricultural land use, no taxa responded positively.
source: Further, while not all taxa showed significant evidence of declining biodiversity in relation to agricultural land use, no taxa responded positively.
evidence: Summary of taxonomic group responses to land use

claim: Planted forests, which were predominantly Pinus radiata plantations, are sometimes perceived as being biologically depauperate.
source: Planted forests, which were predominantly Pinus radiata plantations, are sometimes perceived as being biologically depauperate, while low-producing grasslands are frequently perceived as semi-natural in New Zealand (Hobbs et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement about perceptions supported by citation

claim: Low-producing grasslands are frequently perceived as semi-natural in New Zealand.
source: Planted forests, which were predominantly Pinus radiata plantations, are sometimes perceived as being biologically depauperate, while low-producing grasslands are frequently perceived as semi-natural in New Zealand (Hobbs et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement about perceptions supported by citation

claim: Rarity and diversity in planted forest sites were similar to those in low-producing grassland sites and higher than those in high-producing grassland or perennial cropland sites.
source: Despite this, we found rarity and diversity in planted forest sites to be similar to those in low-producing grassland sites and higher than those in high-producing grassland or perennial cropland sites, consistent with suggestions that plantations can play an important role in insect biodiversity conservation (Pawson et al., 2009; Pawson et al., 2010).
evidence: Summary of biodiversity patterns across land uses

claim: Plantations can play an important role in insect biodiversity conservation.
source: Despite this, we found rarity and diversity in planted forest sites to be similar to those in low-producing grassland sites and higher than those in high-producing grassland or perennial cropland sites, consistent with suggestions that plantations can play an important role in insect biodiversity conservation (Pawson et al., 2009; Pawson et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Perennial cropland supports the lowest levels of invertebrate diversity and rarity of any of the measured land-use categories.
source: Nonetheless, our data suggest perennial cropland supports the lowest levels of invertebrate diversity and rarity of any of the measured land-use categories.
evidence: Summary of biodiversity patterns across land uses

claim: The low biodiversity in perennial cropland may reflect high chemical input in and intensive management of fruit production systems.
source: This may reflect high chemical input in and intensive management of fruit production systems (Manktelow et al., 2005).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to prior research

claim: The results suggest pervasive impacts of agricultural land use upon soil invertebrate communities, with likely adverse consequences for ecosystem services.
source: Overall, our results suggest pervasive impacts of agricultural land use upon soil invertebrate communities, with likely adverse consequences for ecosystem services.
evidence: Synthesis of results with inference about ecosystem consequences

claim: The results add to widespread evidence of declines in invertebrate biomass and diversity in response to anthropogenic land-use change and habitat loss.
source: This adds to widespread evidence of declines in invertebrate biomass and diversity in response to anthropogenic land-use change and habitat loss (Attwood et al., 2008; Hallmann et al., 2017; Hendrickx et al., 2007; Powney et al., 2019), and suggests that efforts to conserve and restore soil invertebrate communities may be needed.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Efforts to conserve and restore soil invertebrate communities may be needed.
source: This adds to widespread evidence of declines in invertebrate biomass and diversity in response to anthropogenic land-use change and habitat loss (Attwood et al., 2008; Hallmann et al., 2017; Hendrickx et al., 2007; Powney et al., 2019), and suggests that efforts to conserve and restore soil invertebrate communities may be needed.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings

claim: Invertebrates tend to be neglected by conservation initiatives, due to the challenges of determining their identities, functions, and distributions.
source: Invertebrates tend to be neglected by conservation initiatives, due to the challenges of determining their identities, functions, and distributions (Leandro et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research

claim: Indirect preservation of communities via flagship or umbrella species protection schemes tends to be ineffective.
source: Indirect preservation of communities via flagship or umbrella species protection schemes tends to be ineffective (Andelman and Fagan, 2000; Oberprieler et al., 2019; Schuldt and Assmann, 2010), and similarly, biomonitoring based on individual species is problematic.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Biomonitoring based on individual species is problematic.
source: Indirect preservation of communities via flagship or umbrella species protection schemes tends to be ineffective (Andelman and Fagan, 2000; Oberprieler et al., 2019; Schuldt and Assmann, 2010), and similarly, biomonitoring based on individual species is problematic.
evidence: Statement based on ecological knowledge

claim: DNA metabarcoding methods may enable more informative biomonitoring and improved targeting of conservation initiatives based on multiple invertebrate taxa.
source: By allowing the efficient assessment of invertebrate community composition and distribution across large spatial scales, DNA metabarcoding methods may enable more informative biomonitoring and improved targeting of conservation initiatives based on multiple invertebrate taxa, if not entire invertebrate communities.
evidence: Inference about potential applications of DNA metabarcoding

claim: Consideration of rarity and phylogenetic rarity alongside richness and phylogenetic measures of diversity would provide the most comprehensive information for purposes such as biomonitoring and conservation planning.
source: While rarity and phylogenetic rarity were the most informative metrics of community change in this case, it is likely that consideration of these alongside richness and phylogenetic measures of diversity would provide the most comprehensive information for purposes such as biomonitoring and conservation planning (Fleishman et al., 2006).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to prior research

claim: Conserving a network of sites with high invertebrate diversity and rarity would preserve a diverse assemblage of species, communities, and functional traits, thus providing resilience of communities and ecosystem processes to environmental changes.
source: Our results suggest that conserving a network of sites with high invertebrate diversity and rarity would preserve a diverse assemblage of species, communities, and functional traits, thus providing resilience of communities and ecosystem processes to environmental changes (Balvanera et al., 2006; Yachi and Loreau, 1999).
evidence: Recommendation based on study results and supported by citations

claim: Diversity and rarity was typically highest in natural forest sites.
source: While diversity and rarity was typically highest in our natural forest sites (of which many are protected), certain grassland and cropland sites with unusually high rarity values (outliers on Figure 3) might be logical targets for further investigation and potential incorporation into conservation initiatives.
evidence: Summary of biodiversity patterns

claim: Certain grassland and cropland sites with unusually high rarity values might be logical targets for further investigation and potential incorporation into conservation initiatives.
source: While diversity and rarity was typically highest in our natural forest sites (of which many are protected), certain grassland and cropland sites with unusually high rarity values (outliers on Figure 3) might be logical targets for further investigation and potential incorporation into conservation initiatives.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings

claim: Most soil invertebrate taxa have consistent rarity responses to land use.
source: In conclusion, our analysis of soil invertebrate biodiversity across land-use categories at a national scale shows that most soil invertebrate taxa have consistent rarity responses to land use, and that agricultural land use tends to cause the homogenisation and loss of soil invertebrate biodiversity.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: Agricultural land use tends to cause the homogenisation and loss of soil invertebrate biodiversity.
source: In conclusion, our analysis of soil invertebrate biodiversity across land-use categories at a national scale shows that most soil invertebrate taxa have consistent rarity responses to land use, and that agricultural land use tends to cause the homogenisation and loss of soil invertebrate biodiversity.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: The impacts of anthropogenic land use on invertebrate biodiversity may have been underestimated due to a widespread emphasis on species richness.
source: This research adds to evidence of widespread impacts of anthropogenic land use on invertebrate biodiversity, but also implies that these impacts may have been underestimated due to a widespread emphasis on species richness.
evidence: Inference based on study findings

claim: DNA metabarcoding methods offer an efficient basis for measuring the diversity and rarity of invertebrate communities at large scales.
source: DNA metabarcoding methods offer an efficient basis for measuring the diversity and rarity of invertebrate communities at large scales.
evidence: Statement based on methodological approach used in study

claim: Incorporating DNA metabarcoding information into conservation schemes would enable the protection of a broader range of biodiversity and enhance the preservation of terrestrial ecosystems.
source: Incorporating this information into conservation schemes would enable the protection of a broader range of biodiversity and enhance the preservation of terrestrial ecosystems.
evidence: Recommendation based on study implications

claim: Soil invertebrate communities were sampled from a total of 75 sites distributed across five different major land-use categories throughout New Zealand.
source: Soil invertebrate communities were sampled from a total of 75 sites distributed across five different major land-use categories throughout New Zealand (Figure 6), during dry weather between November 2014 and March 2015.
evidence: Description of sampling design

claim: The five land-use categories (natural forest, planted forest, low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland) represent differing states of anthropogenic modification.
source: The five land-use categories (natural forest, planted forest, low-producing grassland, high-producing grassland, and perennial cropland) represent differing states of anthropogenic modification (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Description of land-use categories

claim: For each land-use category, 15 replicate sites were randomly selected from the nationwide monitoring grid.
source: For each land-use category, 15 replicate sites were randomly selected from the nationwide monitoring grid, excluding any that were >1000 m altitude and ensuring they were distributed across the length of New Zealand (Makiola et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of site selection methodology

claim: Twenty-four soil cores were collected within each plot on a regular grid to a depth of 15 cm using a sterile corer (5.08 cm diameter).
source: Twenty-four soil cores were collected within each plot on a regular grid (min 3.54 m distance between cores) to a depth of 15 cm using a sterile corer (5.08 cm diameter), following Wood et al. (2017).
evidence: Description of sampling methodology

claim: COI barcodes were amplified by PCR from each sample using metazoan-targeted primers mICOIintF and HCO2198.
source: COI barcodes were amplified by PCR from each sample using metazoan-targeted primers mICOIintF (5'-GGWACWGGWTGAACWGTWTAYCCYCC-3') (Leray et al., 2013) and HCO2198 (5'-TAAACTTCAGGGTGACCAAAAAATCA-3') (Folmer et al., 1994), which were respectively modified at their 5' ends with the linker sequences 5'-TCGTCGGCAGCGTC-3' and 5'-GTCTCGTGGGCTCGG-3'.
evidence: Description of molecular methodology

claim: Non-singleton sequences were clustered into OTUs at a sequence identity threshold of 97%.
source: The trimmed sequences were quality filtered to remove any with >1 maximum expected errors and dereplicated using VSEARCH (Rognes et al., 2016). Non-singleton sequences (i.e. those represented by at least two identical sequences) were clustered into OTUs at a sequence identity threshold of 97% and simultaneously filtered for chimeras using the UPARSE algorithm in USEARCH (Edgar, 2013).
evidence: Description of bioinformatic methodology

claim: The OTUs were assigned a taxonomic identity using the RDP Naïve Bayesian classifier in combination with an RDP-formatted animal mitochondrial COI sequence database.
source: The OTUs were assigned a taxonomic identity using the RDP Naïve Bayesian classifier (Wang et al., 2007) in combination with an RDP-formatted animal mitochondrial COI sequence database (Porter and Hajibabaei, 2018), which includes bacterial, fungal, and protist COI sequences to enable the detection of non-metazoan OTUs.
evidence: Description of taxonomic assignment methodology

claim: Rarity represents the number of OTUs per sample adjusted for their occurrence across all samples.
source: To calculate rarity, a weighting factor (w) was determined for each OTU as the reciprocal of its occurrence across all samples (regardless of land use), so that w = 1 for OTUs that occur in only in a single sample, and w approaches zero for OTUs that occur in many samples. For each sample, values of w were then summed for all OTUs occurring in that sample. In other words, rarity represents the number of OTUs per sample adjusted for their occurrence across all samples (Kier et al., 2009; Kier and Barthlott, 2001).
evidence: Description of rarity calculation methodology

claim: Phylogenetic rarity was calculated as the branch length unique to each sample based on occurrences across all samples.
source: Phylogenetic rarity, in the form of the branch length unique to each sample (based on occurrences across all samples), was calculated for each taxonomic group and sample according to Rosauer et al. (2009) using the R function phylo.endemism (Niperess, 2010).
evidence: Description of phylogenetic rarity calculation methodology

claim: Land-use changes through deforestation, agricultural development, and urbanisation have caused worldwide impacts on the biodiversity of terrestrial communities and ecosystems.
source: Land-use changes through deforestation, agricultural development, and urbanisation have caused worldwide impacts on the biodiversity of terrestrial communities and ecosystems (Dirzo et al., 2014; Newbold et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Invertebrates are the most diverse and abundant component of animal biodiversity worldwide.
source: Invertebrates are the most diverse and abundant component of animal biodiversity worldwide and are major contributors of terrestrial ecosystem services such as pollination, soil formation, and nutrient cycling (Lavelle et al., 2006; Wagg et al., 2014; Yang and Gratton, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Invertebrates are major contributors of terrestrial ecosystem services such as pollination, soil formation, and nutrient cycling.
source: Invertebrates are the most diverse and abundant component of animal biodiversity worldwide and are major contributors of terrestrial ecosystem services such as pollination, soil formation, and nutrient cycling (Lavelle et al., 2006; Wagg et al., 2014; Yang and Gratton, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Long-term declines in the richness and biomass of insects and other terrestrial invertebrates are predicted to have major impacts on food webs and ecosystem functions.
source: Long-term declines in the richness and biomass of insects and other terrestrial invertebrates are predicted to have major impacts on food webs and ecosystem functions (Eisenhauer et al., 2019; Hallmann et al., 2017; Potts et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Most invertebrate species remain undescribed.
